Full detail — every company, ranked (with sourced A / B / C commentary)

#1 NVIDIA NVDA · NASDAQ
Edge 9Capacity 9Track 10S · 93$4,722.4B · 18.6x · Fair
The closest thing to an indispensable 'brains + training + simulation' layer for the humanoid/robot wave — its full stack (Jetson Thor, Isaac GR00T, Isaac Sim, Cosmos, Newton, Omniverse) is genuinely unmatched and nearly every major maker builds on some part of it. The one caveat: robotics revenue is immaterial today, so this is a high-conviction option on a future market, plus the on-robot compute layer is contestable (Qualcomm/Tesla custom silicon).

A · Leading-Edge — 9/10

  • Full 'three-computers' stack — train (DGX), simulate (Omniverse/Isaac Sim), act (Jetson Thor, 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS) — that no rival offers integrated; the moat is architecture + CUDA-X/Isaac software, not fabs (it's fabless). ↗
  • Isaac GR00T humanoid foundation models shipping and iterating (N1.5→N2); Newton physics engine (with DeepMind/Disney) an 'open' tool that still runs best on NVIDIA — classic embrace strategy. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 9/10

  • Marquee customers build on it — Figure, Boston Dynamics, Agility, Hexagon AEON; the sim-to-real data flywheel (Cosmos + Isaac) attacks the industry's #1 bottleneck (real-robot data scarcity). ↗
  • Funds robotics R&D from an ~$80B+/quarter datacenter cash engine — can subsidize the ecosystem for years. But pure robotics is a rounding error vs datacenter today. ↗

C · Track Record — 10/10

  • Datacenter AI is the definitive proof it can seize and OWN a new compute market (GPU-maker → the AI substrate); it is deliberately re-running the CUDA playbook in robotics.
  • Even would-be defectors validate it — Tesla scrapped Dojo (Aug 2025) and leans back on NVIDIA/AMD. ↗

Risks / bear case

  • Materiality/hype gap — robotics revenue negligible; priced on a 5-10 yr market.
  • On-robot compute contestable (Qualcomm Dragonwing, Tesla AI5/AI6); 'open' models (Cosmos/Newton/GR00T) increasingly portable.
#2 Intuitive Surgical ISRG · NASDAQ
Edge 9Capacity 8Track 9S · 87$143.8B · 13.4x · Fair
The single most-validated embodied-AI robotics platform on the market — a profitable, cash-generative, decades-lead incumbent whose installed base, recurring-instrument model and unmatched surgical dataset compound into a genuine moat. Edge 7Capacity 10Track 8S · 84$1,546.8B · 15.7x · Fair
Frontier in ambition and architecture, overhyped on current capability. The genuinely hard-to-copy edge is prospective: auto-scale manufacturing intent + a unified custom-silicon/end-to-end-AI stack. But zero external units, ~90% miss on its 2025 build target, and persistent teleoperation doubts mean the moat is on paper, not in the field.

A · Leading-Edge — 7/10

  • Designs its own actuators, motors, custom silicon (AI5/AI6) and packs in-house — deeper vertical integration than Boston Dynamics (Hyundai Mobis actuators) or Unitree (off-the-shelf RealSense). Edge is cost-at-scale intent, not raw capability today. ↗
  • Gen-3 hand: 22 DoF, ~25 actuators relocated into the forearm, tendon drive, fingertip force sensors — architecturally leading-edge on paper, but still pre-mass-production and unproven. ↗
  • Killed Dojo (Aug 2025, 'evolutionary dead end') and consolidated on AI5/AI6 — credible strategic silicon, but the Dojo failure is a live execution-risk signal. ↗
  • Reuses the FSD end-to-end vision stack and fleet data — real for navigation/vision, but driving data transfers poorly to bimanual manipulation, the actually-hard problem. Partly hype. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 10/10

  • The single most defensible structural edge: auto-scale manufacturing intent — Fremont ex-Model S/X line targeting ~1M/yr pilot, a dedicated 5.2M sq ft Giga Texas plant aimed at 10M/yr. No competitor is building humanoid lines at auto scale. ↗
  • Capital, custom silicon, energy and autonomy adjacencies give Tesla the broadest surface to attack the whole embodied-AI opportunity (humanoid + robotaxi launched 2025 + energy).
  • AI6 explicitly designed to run FSD inference and humanoid autonomy plus training — a shared platform few can match. ↗

C · Track Record — 8/10

  • Elite track record of entering and creating new markets: mass-market EVs, stationary storage (Megapack), the FSD program, and forcing its NACS plug to become the US charging standard. Tesla moves first and aggressively.
  • But Optimus delivery specifically is a chronicle of slippage: 2025 built a few hundred vs a 5,000 target (<10%); Gen-3 reveal slipped again to mid-2026; zero external sales. ↗
  • Musk conceded deployed units are 'primarily for learning and data collection rather than performing productive tasks' (Q4-2025 call) — motion, but not yet productive work. ↗

Risks / bear case

  • Structural timeline slippage — every Optimus milestone since 2021 has slipped.
  • Teleoperation/transparency gap — the Dec-2025 demo fall reignited credible doubts about autonomy.
  • Key-man + leadership churn (Optimus eng. head Milan Kovac left Jun-2025); Figure/Unitree have real deployed units.
#2 Xiaomi — CyberOne / robotics 1810 · HKEX
Edge 5Capacity 9Track 9A · 78$72.1B · 1.1x · Cheap (kicker)
A serious emerging robotics builder wrapped in a marketing halo. Robots are demos/internal 'interns' today and trail Unitree/Tesla on raw performance — but Xiaomi's world-class manufacturing, capital and unmatched record of entering new markets make it a credible 5-year option, scored up for capacity and agility, not current tech.

A · Leading-Edge — 5/10

  • All CyberOne tech is self-developed (in-house AI stack + custom servos from the Xiaomi Robotics Lab) — genuine vertical integration, not a rebadged platform. ↗
  • CyberGear actuators are real and commercialized (sold on AliExpress) but light-duty (~12 N·m) — proves capability, not frontier high-torque humanoid actuation. ↗
  • Differentiated R&D touches (full-palm tactile bionic hand ~8,200 mm², 'bionic sweat-gland' liquid cooling) — but shown only in a controlled investor demo, not independent teardowns. ↗
  • On raw performance CyberOne V2 (0.98 m/s, 3 kg single-arm) trails Unitree H2 (3.3 m/s, 7-15 kg) — a fast follower, not the frontier.

B · Opportunity Capacity — 9/10

  • Beijing EV 'Hyperfactory': 700+ robots, 100% automation across 200+ processes, a 9,100-ton HyperCasting machine, 76-sec cycle — a built-in, hard testbed and cost engine for humanoids few startups can match. ↗
  • Capital and commitment: >RMB200bn group R&D over 5 years from 2026 (RMB60bn on AI); EV scale, smart-home install base and Mi-Sense perception data as latent advantages. ↗
  • FY2025 revenue RMB457.3bn (+25%) funds the push internally — robotics doesn't need to pay its own way yet. ↗

C · Track Record — 9/10

  • Best track record of seizing new markets of anyone in this category: phones → a vast IoT ecosystem → EVs (SU7) reaching profitability in record time. Xiaomi enters and wins. ↗
  • Already invested externally in embodied AI (Xiaoyu Intelligent Manufacturing, 2023) and stood up a Robotics Lab — more than halo theater.
  • But robotics specifically is immature: CyberOne isn't for sale, CyberDog 2 is a ~$1,800 enthusiast toy, and factory trials are 'intern'-level (90.2% success, ~3 hrs autonomous). ↗

Risks / bear case

  • Robotics is financially immaterial — no separately disclosed revenue; near-zero P&L impact.
  • Halo-project risk — investor-day demos optimize for narrative; capability lags claims.
  • Trails Unitree/Tesla/Figure/UBTech on robot performance — a fast follower.
#3 Estun Automation 002747 · Shenzhen / HKEX
Edge 6Capacity 7Track 7B · 67$4.4B · 6.6x · Fair
A strong, vertically-integrated fast-follower edging toward the frontier — not a frontier innovator. Gains are ~60% cost/integration import-substitution, ~40% technology; still depends on Japanese reducers. But it moves aggressively (M&A, exports, humanoid components), which is what counts here.

A · Leading-Edge — 6/10

  • One of very few robot makers that designs servo drives, servo motors, controllers and CNC in-house ('all-in-one') — structurally rare and a real cost/tuning edge. ↗
  • Trio (UK, 2017) gives genuine motion-PLC IP sold to third-party OEMs; Cloos (Germany) is a defensible high-end arc-welding position with European customers. ↗
  • Key gap: still relies on Nabtesco RV / Harmonic Drive reducers — the highest-value, hardest-to-localize component is NOT internalized; domestic dual-sourcing is mainly for price leverage. ↗
  • ~610 patents (258 invention) — solid for a Chinese OEM but incremental engineering depth, not a fundamental lead over Fanuc/Yaskawa.

B · Opportunity Capacity — 7/10

  • Vertical integration plus expanding surface: welding (Cloos), CNC, and a 2025 humanoid component effort (Codroid 02) leveraging its joint-module/servo stack for torque density.
  • Export push is real and margin-accretive — overseas ~34% of 2024 revenue at ~32% gross margin (vs ~26% domestic); Poland factory completed 2025. ↗
  • Capacity capped by wafer-thin profitability and capital dependence (discounted Mar-2026 HK IPO). ↗

C · Track Record — 7/10

  • #1 domestic robot brand by shipments for 7 straight years; >10% China share in Q1-2025 and rising as domestic brands hit ~40% of China volume. ↗
  • Demonstrated agility via aggressive M&A (Trio, Cloos), global build-out, and an early humanoid pivot — it consistently moves into adjacencies.
  • But execution quality is thin: 2024 net loss ~RMB810M (incl. ~RMB360M impairment); 2025 barely positive (~RMB41M) on RMB4B+ revenue. ↗

Risks / bear case

  • Wafer-thin profitability + intensifying China price war.
  • Reducer dependence on Japan caps cost control and is a supply chokepoint.
  • Capital dependence — discounted HK listing signals investor skepticism.
#4 UBTech Robotics 9880 · HKEX
Edge 5Capacity 7Track 8B · 67$5.3B · 16.0x · Rich
A credible top-tier commercializer aggressively seizing the factory-humanoid opportunity — but early, not a proven frontier technology leader, and richly priced. Deepest humanoid patent stack and real OEM deployments, but commoditizing hardware, an AI stack trailing Figure, and its own admission that Walker S2 is ≤50% as productive as a human.

A · Leading-Edge — 5/10

  • Genuine in-house servo actuators (~1M cumulative) — but exactly where China's dense supply chain erodes the moat (a China-sourced humanoid actuator ~$22K vs ~$58K without Chinese parts; advantage accrues to China broadly). ↗
  • 2,985 authorized patents (Dec-2025) — cited as the global leader in effective humanoid patents; the strongest single defensibility claim, though China patent counts overstate enforceable moat. ↗
  • Walker S2's 3-minute autonomous battery swap is a real, verified engineering feat for uptime — but the AI stack (BrainNet/Co-Agent) shows no evidence of matching Figure's Helix generalization. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 7/10

  • Manufacturing + OEM relationships in place; mass production launched Nov-2025, capacity targets 5,000 (2026) and 10,000 (2027) units. Real capacity to scale, though capital-constrained. ↗
  • Diversified legacy revenue (logistics ¥629M, consumer ¥499M) cushions the humanoid push, but persistent negative FCF means reliance on equity raises. ↗

C · Track Record — 8/10

  • Aggressively moved across categories: toys → education → logistics → humanoids. Full-size humanoid revenue jumped 22x to ¥821M in FY2025 (now its largest line); 1,079 units sold. ↗
  • Walker S on real automaker lines — BYD, NIO, Zeekr, Geely, FAW-VW, Audi FAW, Dongfeng, plus Foxconn/SF Express — and ~¥800M+ order book. Genuine, if early/soft, traction. ↗
  • Caveat: many 'deployments' are pilots/data-collection (some orders from data-collection centers — circular); FY2025 net loss ¥790M.

Risks / bear case

  • Cash burn + dilution + ~16x sales valuation pricing a frontier-leader outcome.
  • Demo-vs-reality gap — ≤50% human productivity by its own admission.
  • Brutal Chinese competition — Unitree (5,500+ units) and AgiBot (5,168) out-ship it; hardware commoditizing.
#5 FANUC 6954 · Tokyo
Edge 7Capacity 7Track 4B · 60$42.0B · 7.1x · Fair
A fortress incumbent — leading-edge and defensible at the high end, maturing at the low end — but its conservative, closed culture is exactly the 'rarely moves' profile that scores low on seizing. The 2025-26 Google/NVIDIA Physical-AI pivot is smart but partner-led: Fanuc is renting the AI brains.

A · Leading-Edge — 7/10

  • Full vertical integration (servo → drive → controller → vision → robot) yields ~80,000-hr MTBF and ~21% operating margins competitors can't match — a decades-deep systems-engineering moat, not one patent. ↗
  • CNC near-monopoly (~50-60% global high-end share) with high switching costs and a large maintenance annuity from 5M+ CNCs — durable at the top, eroding at the bottom to Chinese GSK/HuazhongCNC. ↗
  • Largest installed base on Earth: 1.1M+ robots + 5M+ CNCs — increasingly a data/AI moat, not just service. ↗
  • AI intelligence is rented, not owned: Google (Gemini/Intrinsic, May-2026) and NVIDIA (Isaac/GR00T/Jetson Thor) supply the brains — ceding software value to Big Tech. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 7/10

  • Installed base + capital + Physical-AI partnerships give real capacity to capture the factory-automation-AI opportunity (1,000+ Physical-AI robots shipped since late-2025). ↗
  • But deliberately no humanoid program and a narrow factory-arm/CNC surface — it positions as the arms/brains layer, not an opportunity-expander.
  • Record FY2025 (sales ¥857.8B, +7.6%; ~21.4% margin) and FY2026 guidance up — but the growth engine (China EV capex) is also its biggest competitive threat. ↗

C · Track Record — 4/10

  • Famously conservative, closed, hardware-led cadence — the textbook 'leading-edge but rarely moves into new markets' profile.
  • Recent openness (ROS 2 driver for CRX cobots, Google/NVIDIA tie-ups) is real but reactive and partner-dependent, not self-driven market creation. ↗
  • No new-category creation in years; the Physical-AI move is its first genuine strategic pivot in a long time.

Risks / bear case

  • China share loss — Estun (~9.5%) and Inovance (~8.8%) now rival Fanuc's ~11% China share.
  • Deep auto/electronics capex cyclicality (robot sales swung ~-16% in the prior down-leg).
  • AI brains rented from Google/NVIDIA — cedes the software-era value layer.
#6 Yaskawa Electric 6506 · Tokyo
Edge 7Capacity 6Track 5B · 60$11.3B · 3.5x · Fair
A high-quality incumbent making a genuine, NVIDIA-enabled bid to stay leading-edge — more proactive than Fanuc lately (MOTOMAN NEXT, SoftBank, US plant), but the moat is narrowing in China and robotics economics are thinning.

A · Leading-Edge — 7/10

  • World #1 AC servo position on 65+ years of in-house IP (>20M cumulative units, 23-bit encoders) — vertical integration of motor/encoder/drive is the moat. Durable at the high end, eroding in commodity tiers. ↗
  • Shared servo/drive tech amortizes across motion-control AND Motoman robots — a structural advantage pure-play robot makers lack; now extending to SiC inverters. ↗
  • >600,000 Motoman robots installed (global 'Big Four') create switching costs in auto welding. ↗
  • MOTOMAN NEXT — industry-'first adaptive robot,' open platform on NVIDIA Jetson Orin + Isaac — a genuine architectural step toward unstructured-environment autonomy. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 6/10

  • Diversifying beyond auto into semiconductor, machine tools, biomedical, logistics; AI/data-center capex now a tailwind (servos for chip tools, inverters for DC cooling).
  • SoftBank 'Physical AI' partnership (Dec-2025) for an office robot signals ambition beyond the factory and telecom-grade edge AI — early, not yet revenue. ↗
  • Capacity capped by reliance on NVIDIA for the AI layer and thinning robotics margins.

C · Track Record — 5/10

  • More proactive than peers recently: launched MOTOMAN NEXT, opened first US high-volume robot plant (Wisconsin), $180M servo expansion — genuine moves. ↗
  • But robotics segment margin slipped 10.0%→8.3% on low-value China auto projects — pricing power weakest where volume is rising. ↗
  • No humanoid product — cedes that frontier narrative while leaning on NVIDIA's stack.

Risks / bear case

  • Chinese servo erosion — Inovance >26% of China's domestic servo market.
  • Low-quality robotics growth + capex cyclicality.
  • Frontier/humanoid execution unproven; NVIDIA-dependent.
#7 ABB — Robotics div. (→ SoftBank) ABBN · SIX / NYSE: ABBNY
Edge 6Capacity 5Track 4C · 50$191.9B · 5.5x · Fair
A top-2 franchise with one real software moat (OmniCore) and durable paint/weld IP, wrapped around a commoditizing arm and a structurally low-margin P&L. The decisive signal is corporate: ABB sequentially de-risked OUT of robotics — spin-off, then an outright $5.375B sale to SoftBank (Oct-2025). It chose NOT to seize.

A · Leading-Edge — 6/10

  • OmniCore control platform (~$170M invested): <0.6mm path accuracy, 1,600mm/s, 25% faster / 20% less energy — control software/motion IP is the stickiest, least-commoditized layer. ↗
  • Decades of paint/weld process IP (auto paint shops) is application-specific and hard to copy — a real niche moat tied to a cyclical end-market. ↗
  • AI 3D-VSLAM via Sevensense (ETH spin-off) outperforms 2D-laser nav (deployed at Ford/Michelin) — differentiated but young in a fast-moving field. ↗
  • The robot arm itself is commoditizing fastest; AI/vision add-ons are becoming table stakes.

B · Opportunity Capacity — 5/10

  • As an asset under SoftBank's Physical-AI thesis, capacity could rise (capital + ambition). But under ABB it was sub-scale to the group (~7% of revenue, 12.1% EBITA vs ~18% group). ↗
  • ABB explicitly cited 'limited business and technology synergies' — i.e. it saw no reason to invest in the opportunity itself. ↗

C · Track Record — 4/10

  • Restrained on humanoids and strategically inconsistent: spin-off (Apr-2025) → reclassified → outright sale (Oct-2025). Robotics President departs by end-2026. ↗
  • Sub-par margins and missed guidance (Q1-2025 orders missed by ~$260M) — execution mixed. ↗
  • The clearest 'did NOT seize' case in the category — it sold the franchise rather than build on it.

Risks / bear case

  • China competition — Inovance/Estun/Efort undercut 20-30%; domestic makers outsold foreign rivals for the first time in 9M-2025.
  • Auto cyclicality + sub-par (12%) margins.
  • Ownership/integration/regulatory risk before the mid-late-2026 SoftBank close.

A · Leading-Edge — 5/10

  • In-house 6-axis torque sensors + top-tier PL(e)/Cat-4 safety — good engineering, but replicable (UR, FANUC CRX, Techman clear comparable bars; torque sensing is table stakes). ↗
  • Dart-Suite app-store software mirrors UR's UR+/Polyscope — a fast-follow, not a first-mover moat; network effects early and small. ↗

  • But sub-scale and shrinking — capacity to attack new opportunity is constrained by a deteriorating core (FY2025 revenue ~$24M, -29.6%; operating loss widened 44%). ↗

C · Track Record — 4/10

  • Has expanded (US HQ + ONExia acquisition, F&B series, humanoid roadmap) — moves, but doesn't deliver: revenue down ~30%, losses widening, sub-scale vs UR/FANUC.
  • Better-capitalized Korean rival Samsung-backed Rainbow Robotics is encroaching; Doosan's humanoid revenue is years out (2028) and execution-risky. ↗

Risks / bear case

  • ~130x EV/Sales against shrinking revenue and ~7% gross margin — extreme.
  • Cobots commoditizing fast (UR/FANUC/Techman + Chinese JAKA/AUBO/Elite price war).
  • Sub-scale with deepening losses; Samsung/Rainbow competition at home.

Edge 3Capacity 5Track 6D · 47$0.3B · 2.9x · Fair
A capable automation distributor + systems integrator riding the robotics theme — NOT a frontier robotics-technology owner. Its own product pages label the key components ('代理' = distributed): it resells Harmonic Drive reducers, Nabtesco, Nidec, and even UBTech humanoids. Value-add is integration, not invention.

A · Leading-Edge — 3/10

  • Harmonic reducers are NOT in-house — Aurotek's page states it 'distributes/agents' Harmonic Drive; the robotics catalog is a ~20-brand distribution list (Nabtesco, Nidec, DENSO, DOBOT…). ↗
  • Genuinely proprietary lines are narrow and commoditized: own-brand PCB depaneling machines and AOI optical inspection — real, but not frontier robotics. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 5/10

  • Integration know-how + broad channel (1,000+ accounts across semiconductor/EMS, logistics, F&B) and a pivot to 'AI robot integration solutions' — but no core tech to scale into new markets. ↗
  • Riding AI-server/semicap capex; prior years were an 'operating trough,' so durability is unproven.

C · Track Record — 6/10

  • Strong recent execution — FY2025 revenue NT$2.50bn (+50%), profitable (EPS NT$2.08), 1Q26 +58.7% — and a clear strategic pivot. Good agility for an integrator. ↗
  • But 'seizing' here means reselling/integrating others' robots — originality is low and margins depend on principals who can disintermediate.

Risks / bear case

  • No proprietary core-component moat — depends on Harmonic Drive/Nabtesco/UBTech/DOBOT.
  • Small scale (~US$300m) + retail-press 'robotics-purity' froth; thin Chinese-only disclosure.
  • Cyclicality — the surge rides AI-server capex off a trough.

Full detail — traceable logic

#1 Novanta NOVT · NASDAQ
Edge 8Capacity 8Track 8S · 80$5.6B · 5.5x · Fair
The highest-quality name in the category — proprietary sub-micron feedback IP, ~45% gross margins, net cash, and an 'arms-dealer' position selling the encoders every robot and surgical robot needs. Near-term organic growth is soft, so it's priced for execution.

A · Leading-Edge — 8/10

  • Ultra-high-res optical/inductive encoders, air-bearing spindles, frameless motors and force/torque sensors — sub-micron feedback that is genuinely hard to replicate. ↗
  • ~45.6% non-GAAP gross margin — ~15 pts above Allient — is the clearest proof of real pricing power and proprietary IP.

B · Opportunity Capacity — 8/10

  • >1/3 of the business is robotics/automation, with an explicit humanoid encoder offering for whole-body coordination/joint alignment. ↗
  • Joined the NVIDIA Halos AI systems inspection lab; encoders are the indispensable feedback layer across robot OEMs. ↗

C · Track Record — 8/10

  • Compounded to ~$1B revenue via disciplined acquisitions of IP-rich niche leaders (Celera Motion et al.), holding high margins through cycles.
  • Q1'26 bookings +37% YoY, book-to-bill 1.10, FY26 outlook raised — though organic growth is only ~+3% and EPS guide sits below consensus. ↗

Risks / bear case

  • Rich valuation prices in robotics optionality; soft organic growth could compress the multiple.
  • Medical-end-market cyclicality + acquisition-integration risk.
#2 Inovance Technology 300124 · Shenzhen
Edge 7Capacity 8Track 9S · 80$26.0B · 4.0x · Fair
The rare Chinese industrial champion whose share gains rest on a genuinely integrated motion stack, not just price — and the best-positioned domestic incumbent to convert that stack into humanoid-actuator volume. High-end precision still trails Japan and it doesn't own the reducer bottleneck.

A · Leading-Edge — 7/10

  • ~28-32% of China's servo market (#1, ahead of Yaskawa/Mitsubishi locally) built on in-house control loops, not just price. ↗
  • Near-complete in-house stack: servo drives + motors + controllers + PLC/HMI + 97%-efficiency PMSMs + frameless torque motors. But tops out at 23-bit encoders vs Yaskawa's 26-bit, and is weak in large PLCs (Siemens ~44%). ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 8/10

  • Dedicated humanoid team since 2023; developing rotary+linear joint modules, frameless torque motors, roller screws and integrated actuators — a shipping joint already deployed in Blueye warehouse robots. ↗
  • Mass-manufacturing cost edge as humanoid volumes inflect; names 'Intelligent Robots' as a next golden track. Caveat: buys harmonic reducers from Shuanghuan/Leader — doesn't own the bottleneck. ↗

C · Track Record — 9/10

  • Took servo share from single digits to #1 over a decade; 9M25 revenue ¥31.7B (+25%), outgrowing a soft cycle. ↗
  • Scaled NEV powertrain from zero to multi-billion (AAM JV); building Hungary plant + Stuttgart R&D — a documented serial seizer. ↗

#1 Hesai Group HSAI · NASDAQ/HK

Genuinely leading-edge: a seven-component in-house ASIC stack, #1 lidar patent portfolio, and category-best ~42% gross margin let it wage the price war profitably. But it's now a profitable-scale play, not a monopoly — ASPs are deflating, RoboSense already out-ships it in robotics, and US delisting/1260H risk is a live tail.

A · Leading-Edge — 8/10

  • Only lidar maker developing all 7 core components in-house; 16 auto-qualified ASICs, ~185M units shipped — the basis for its cost lead; ranked #1 in lidar patents by KnowMade. ↗
  • FY25 gross margin 41.8% vs RoboSense 28.5% and Seyond 7.9% — the moat is economic, letting it launch a ~$200 lidar as offense. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 9/10

  • Robotics deliveries hit 239,273 units in FY25 (+426%); an exclusive 10M-unit JT-series supply deal to Dreame/MOVA mowers; the only lidar name on Morgan Stanley's 'Humanoid Tech 25'. ↗
  • Every Unitree humanoid at the 2026 Gala ran Hesai JT128; doubling capacity to 4M+ units in 2026. But RoboSense out-shipped it in robotics in Q1'26. ↗

C · Track Record — 8/10

  • First lidar pure-play to full-year GAAP profitability (FY25 revenue RMB3.03B +46%, net income RMB436M); 4 straight profitable quarters. ↗
  • Serial early mover — robotaxi → overseas high-end auto → industrial/robotics, entering markets before commoditization; ~37-39% auto-lidar share.

Risks / bear case

  • US geopolitical — on DoD 1260H list, lost its delisting lawsuit; senators pressing for delisting.
  • ASP deflation/price war; lost the robotics volume crown to RoboSense; thin absolute net margin.

Any live 'LAZR' quote is a stale/erroneous OTC artifact — the equity is worthless. Included only as a data point on single-customer concentration + governance failure.

A · Leading-Edge — 5/10

  • Iris/Halo long-range 1550nm lidar was technically credible — the tech wasn't the failure point; MicroVision paid for the lidar IP. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 2/10

  • Essentially none — never diversified into robotics/AMR/industrial the way Ouster did; its Volvo anchor deal was terminated for failure to meet obligations. ↗

C · Track Record — 1/10

  • A near-total execution failure — CEO resigned May 2025 amid an ethics probe, CFO departed, multiple loan defaults, 25% layoffs, SEC inquiry → bankruptcy. ↗

Risks / bear case

  • REALIZED — equity is a zero.
  • Any residual IP value accrues to MicroVision, not LAZR holders.

Full detail — traceable logic

#1 NVIDIA NVDA · NASDAQ
Edge 9Capacity 9Track 10S · 93$4,722.4B · 18.6x · Fair
The closest thing to an indispensable 'brains + training + simulation' layer for the humanoid/robot wave — its full stack (Jetson Thor, Isaac GR00T, Isaac Sim, Cosmos, Newton, Omniverse) is genuinely unmatched and nearly every major maker builds on some part of it. The one caveat: robotics revenue is immaterial today, so this is a high-conviction option on a future market, plus the on-robot compute layer is contestable (Qualcomm/Tesla custom silicon).

A · Leading-Edge — 9/10

  • Full 'three-computers' stack — train (DGX), simulate (Omniverse/Isaac Sim), act (Jetson Thor, 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS) — that no rival offers integrated; the moat is architecture + CUDA-X/Isaac software, not fabs (it's fabless). ↗
  • Isaac GR00T humanoid foundation models shipping and iterating (N1.5→N2); Newton physics engine (with DeepMind/Disney) an 'open' tool that still runs best on NVIDIA — classic embrace strategy. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 9/10

  • Marquee customers build on it — Figure, Boston Dynamics, Agility, Hexagon AEON; the sim-to-real data flywheel (Cosmos + Isaac) attacks the industry's #1 bottleneck (real-robot data scarcity). ↗
  • Funds robotics R&D from an ~$80B+/quarter datacenter cash engine — can subsidize the ecosystem for years. But pure robotics is a rounding error vs datacenter today. ↗

C · Track Record — 10/10

  • Datacenter AI is the definitive proof it can seize and OWN a new compute market (GPU-maker → the AI substrate); it is deliberately re-running the CUDA playbook in robotics.
  • Even would-be defectors validate it — Tesla scrapped Dojo (Aug 2025) and leans back on NVIDIA/AMD. ↗

Risks / bear case

  • Materiality/hype gap — robotics revenue negligible; priced on a 5-10 yr market.
  • On-robot compute contestable (Qualcomm Dragonwing, Tesla AI5/AI6); 'open' models (Cosmos/Newton/GR00T) increasingly portable.
#2 Infineon IFX · XETRA
Edge 8Capacity 7Track 8A · 77$116.3B · 7.2x · Fair
The closest thing to a picks-and-shovels default for the electrification of robots — an IDM leader in the exact power, MCU and sensing content every humanoid needs (it quantifies ~$500 semi BOM/robot), with its own wide-bandgap fabs and a marquee NVIDIA tie-up. But near-term robotics revenue is immaterial and buried inside a cyclically depressed auto/industrial base.

A · Leading-Edge — 8/10

  • #1 in power semis (~17-20%) AND #1 in global MCUs (21.3%) — the two most robot-essential chip categories; a true IDM with its own Si/GaN/SiC fabs (world's largest 200mm SiC fab, Kulim) and first-mover 300mm GaN. ↗
  • Full sense→compute→actuate silicon (XENSIV radar/ToF/current sensors + PSoC/AURIX MCUs + gate/motor drivers + power) — few rivals cover the whole robot BOM. But it's the enabling supplier, not the AI 'brain'. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 7/10

  • Company-quantified ~$500 semiconductor BOM per humanoid; expanded NVIDIA partnership for Jetson Thor humanoids; Marvell auto-Ethernet acquisition adds in-machine networking. ↗
  • But humanoid revenue is immaterial today (robot market ~$2B vs Infineon €14.7B) — content claims are BOM math, not booked wins.

C · Track Record — 8/10

  • Serial category leadership executed (overtook rivals to #1 in MCUs + auto semis); capex-through-cycle discipline (built SiC/GaN capacity during the downturn); pivoted fast to AI-datacenter power (~€1.5B target). ↗
  • Marketing cadence around humanoids outruns disclosed revenue.

Risks / bear case

  • Deep cyclicality — FY25 revenue fell to €14.7B at the low end of its model.
  • Humanoid = optionality on a long fuse; Chinese SiC/MCU competition on margins.
#3 Power Integrations POWI · NASDAQ
Edge 8Capacity 7Track 7A · 73$4.7B · 9.7x · Fair
The quality name among the power-IC group — a real high-voltage IP moat (2,000+ patents, first to volume GaN), profitable through the trough, with legitimate motor-drive robotics content (BridgeSwitch BLDC). But robotics is upside optionality on a slow-growing core, not the current story.

A · Leading-Edge — 8/10

  • Genuine high-voltage IP moat — decades of HV BCD process + system-level integration (InnoSwitch/BridgeSwitch fold controller+FETs+sensing+protection into one IC); profitable (~54% GM) through the trough, unlike GaN pure-plays. ↗
  • PowiGaN is the growth engine (GaN revenue +40%+ FY25). But still dominated by appliances/consumer.

B · Opportunity Capacity — 7/10

  • Direct robotics relevance — BridgeSwitch-2 BLDC motor-driver family targets brushless DC drives to ~1HP at >98.5% efficiency, exactly the actuator/motor-control layer in robots/cobots. ↗
  • But robotics is a slice of 'industrial,' not yet a named needle-mover.

C · Track Record — 7/10

  • Long profitable history, dividend raised for 2026, disciplined ~23% R&D; executes reliably.
  • But growth has been muted — FY25 revenue $443M ~flat vs FY23; the last 18 months are recovery, not a breakout.

Risks / bear case

  • Consumer/appliance cyclicality dominates the top line.
  • GaN commoditization as Navitas/Infineon/EPC/TI scale.
#4 Microchip MCHP · NASDAQ
Edge 7Capacity 8Track 7A · 73$48.3B · 11.4x · Fair
The higher-quality, more defensible embedded name — a sticky MCU franchise with direct motor-control and edge-AI robotics content that just executed a convincing margin/revenue recovery. Tempered by leverage and an inventory downturn that was partly self-created.

A · Leading-Edge — 7/10

  • One of the strongest design-in moats in the industry — sticky PIC/AVR/dsPIC MCUs, huge SKU catalog, long lifecycles, ~120k customers; adds PIC64 8-core RISC-V for autonomous robotics + PolarFire FPGA; ~58.5% GM recovered. ↗
  • Not leading-edge in process node — the moat is breadth + switching costs, not silicon supremacy.

B · Opportunity Capacity — 8/10

  • dsPIC33 DSCs are purpose-built for motor control — the low-level layer of virtually every robot joint; Feb-2026 production-ready full-stack Edge AI (MPLAB ML) targets intelligent robotics/factory automation; supplies most of a robot's electronics BOM below the main SoC. ↗

C · Track Record — 7/10

  • Textbook cyclical recovery — Q4 FY26 net sales $1.31B (+35% YoY), full-year non-GAAP net income +32%; 'nine-point recovery plan' delivered. ↗
  • But the 2024-25 downturn was partly self-inflicted (over-shipped into distribution) — competent cleanup of its own mess.

Risks / bear case

  • Leverage from Microsemi/Atmel deals; dividend + debt paydown compete for cash.
  • MCU competition (ST/Renesas/NXP/Infineon + Chinese entrants).
#5 STMicroelectronics STM · NYSE
Edge 7Capacity 8Track 6A · 70$66.5B · 5.1x · Fair
Owns the broadest robotics BOM footprint (STM32 compute + MEMS/IMU/ToF sensing + motor control + SiC power) and the best developer/NVIDIA on-ramp — but its just-emerged-from-a-brutal-downturn margins and reactive restructuring make it the higher-optionality, lower-execution-quality play vs NXP.

A · Leading-Edge — 7/10

  • IDM owning its fabs (SiC, MEMS); STM32 is the industry-standard 32-bit MCU ecosystem (STM32N6 adds on-chip NPU); owns MEMS/IMU/ToF — the literal 'inner ear and eyes' of a humanoid — plus SiC power for actuators. ↗
  • IDM = cost control, but fabs are the margin liability when utilization collapses.

B · Opportunity Capacity — 8/10

C · Track Record — 6/10

Full detail — traceable logic

#1 Hyundai Motor 005380 · Korea (KRX)
Edge 8Capacity 9Track 7S · 80$64.8B · 1.4x · Cheap (kicker)
The best-positioned legacy OEM in robotics by a wide margin — it uniquely pairs the field's premier locomotion IP (Boston Dynamics), a credible AI stack (DeepMind/TRI/NVIDIA), and captive auto-manufacturing scale plus a first customer to industrialize humanoids. But it's a long-dated option: robotics is immaterial to today's earnings and the lab-to-line leap at 30,000-unit scale is unproven.

A · Leading-Edge — 8/10

  • Electric Atlas moved from R&D to a shipping product (production began at BD's Boston HQ, CES 2026); best-in-class dynamic locomotion remains a durable moat the field can't replicate; AI now credible via BD+Toyota Research large-behavior-models and a Google DeepMind foundation-model partnership. ↗
  • But on deployed productive work, Agility's Digit — not Atlas — is the only humanoid credibly earning revenue; Atlas leads on athleticism, not yet field hours.

B · Opportunity Capacity — 9/10

  • Captive first customer at industrial scale — plans to deploy tens of thousands of BD robots in its own plants; $26B US investment includes a robotics factory sized for 30,000 units/yr by 2028. ↗
  • Broad in-house portfolio de-risks it (Spot 2,000+ units, Stretch at DHL/Maersk/Gap, X-ble exoskeletons); auto-scale manufacturing DNA to industrialize humanoids. ↗

C · Track Record — 7/10

  • Multi-decade commitment (Robotics Lab 2019 → BD acquisition 2021 → CES 2026 strategy); executed Atlas from viral R&D to a shipping product with committed customers — a bar Tesla missed. ↗
  • But BD has been loss-making/subscale; humanoid revenue still ~zero; lab-to-line at 30k scale unproven.

Risks / bear case

  • Materiality tiny — BD ~$130-300M vs Hyundai's ~$135B revenue; a multi-year option.
  • Humanoid commercialization unproven (2028-2030 timelines could slip); auto cyclicality/tariffs.

Edge 5Capacity 9Track 8A · 74$106.6B · 1.1x · Cheap (kicker)
An EV/battery juggernaut whose robotics ambition is real but embryonic — genuine only as optionality riding on unmatched manufacturing, battery, motor and now automotive-silicon/physical-AI capacity. If any incumbent can brute-force a low-cost humanoid via shared components and 97%-automated factories, it's BYD — but underwrite the EV/battery core today, not robotics.

A · Leading-Edge — 5/10

  • Direct humanoid effort is nascent/stealthy (Yao-Shun-Yu program, 2024 recruitment); the genuine leading edge is autonomy — 'God's Eye' ADAS on 2.3M+ vehicles + a next-gen 4nm auto SoC (>2,100 TOPS) whose physical-AI stack transfers to robotics. ↗
  • But defensibility today rests on manufacturing/cost, not robotics IP — it's buying in (AgiBot, PaXini tactile) rather than owning frontier embodied-AI.

B · Opportunity Capacity — 9/10

  • Colossal core to fund a pivot (FY25 revenue ~$116B, 4.5M+ vehicles); shared BOM thesis (batteries + control units + drive motors reused in humanoids); world-class in-house automation (10,000+ robots, ~97% plant autonomy) + BYD Electronic as a ready contract-manufacturer. ↗
  • Deploys others' humanoids (UBTech Walker S) on its lines; could sell household humanoids via its dealer network.

C · Track Record — 8/10

  • Serial category-conqueror (battery → largest EV brand + semis, motors, storage); fast ADAS execution (free God's Eye fleet-wide in ~1 year → in-house 4nm SoC). ↗
  • But robotics moves are small bets/minority stakes, not shipped product; reported humanoid targets unconfirmed.

Risks / bear case

  • Robotics a rounding error today — no revenue, no shipped humanoid; a pivot could be deprioritized as EV margins compress (net profit -19% FY25).
  • Not the frontier on embodied AI; geopolitical/tariff constraints on Western markets.
#3 Uber Technologies UBER · NYSE
Edge 7Capacity 8Track 7A · 73$153.7B · 3.0x · Fair
Owns the single most valuable asset in mobility — aggregated, sticky demand at ~200M users — and is executing a disciplined, cash-generative, asset-light autonomy strategy that makes it the default distribution layer for the dozens of subscale AV developers who can't self-distribute. But its moat is thinnest against the one player that matters most — Waymo's Phoenix exit is a live warning the winning AV builders will disintermediate the network once their own demand is dense enough.

A · Leading-Edge — 7/10

  • Demand aggregation at massive scale is the core moat (Q1'26: 199M MAPCs, 3.64B trips, $53.7B gross bookings) — no AV builder can replicate it overnight; fleet-utilization edge (Waymo-on-Uber vehicles 'busier than 99%' of human drivers) is the AV owner's #1 profit lever, and Uber controls it. ↗
  • But the moat is weakest where it matters — Waymo PULLED its rides off the Uber app in Phoenix (June 2026) and runs standalone; the leader doesn't need Uber's demand. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 8/10

  • AV Mobility trips grew >10x YoY (8 cities → 15 by end-2026); ~30 AV/robotics partners; >$10B committed to robotaxi partnerships/fleets — broadest global AV footprint, seeding demand where Waymo/Tesla won't go for years. ↗
  • But volumes are still trivial vs 3.64B quarterly trips.

C · Track Record — 7/10

  • Well-timed capital-light pivot — sold in-house ATG to Aurora (2020), re-entered as an aggregator; FY25 revenue $52B (+18%), TTM FCF ~$9.8B funds ~$3B/qtr buybacks AND $10B AV bets simultaneously. ↗
  • But it has never controlled its AV destiny — every in-house effort failed; wins depend on partners who can defect.

Risks / bear case

  • Disintermediation by Waymo/Tesla (own tech + fleet + app).
  • AV margin compression; the robotaxi narrative re-rated the stock while AV is immaterial to earnings.
#4 XPeng XPEV · NYSE
Edge 7Capacity 8Track 7A · 73$12.2B · 1.4x · Cheap (kicker)

A · Leading-Edge — 7/10

  • In-house full stack is genuine — IRON runs three self-designed Turing chips (~2,250 TOPS), 2nd-gen VLA/VLM, 82 body DOF + 22/hand, and an industry-first full-solid-state battery, shared with its EVs/robotaxis/eVTOL (Tesla-like vertical integration). ↗
  • But the lifelike demo sparked 'human-in-a-suit' accusations; analysts argue the next-gen IRON 'was NOT on stage'; early factory-trial hands 'didn't last a month' — verified capability lags the demo. ↗

  • Three real embodiment verticals with facilities — IRON humanoid (mass production targeted end-2026), three robotaxi models for 2026, and the AeroHT flying car (trial production, ~5-7k orders); EV core (FY25 revenue RMB76.7B +88%) funds it; supply-chain reuse lowers marginal cost. ↗
  • Risk of spreading thin across three capital-hungry frontier programs while the EV core is barely breakeven.

  • Financial fragility funding three frontier bets in a brutal China EV price war.

B · Opportunity Capacity — 6/10

Risks / bear case

  • Financial distress makes self-funded robotics R&D hard — GoMate could be starved/vaporware.
  • Announcement-heavy, verification-light; 2026 production target unconfirmed.

Full detail — traceable logic

#1 Siemens SIE · XETRA
Edge 9Capacity 8Track 8S · 83$234.4B · 3.2x · Fair
The highest-quality enabler of factory robotics and physical AI — owner of the automation-share lead, the simulation/software spine (Altair, Xcelerator), and the deepest NVIDIA industrial partnership, with a live humanoid pilot to prove it. It won't build the robots, so upside is leveraged and indirect, and near-term results ride a cyclical automation recovery.

A · Leading-Edge — 9/10

  • #1 global factory-automation share (~20%+, ~2x Rockwell/ABB); Simatic PLCs, Sinamics drives and PLC-robot interfaces are the control backbone robots plug into, with high switching costs from installed base + TIA Portal lock-in. ↗
  • ~$10.6B Altair acquisition (largest ever) adds simulation/HPC/AI critical to sim-to-real robot training; NVIDIA 'Industrial AI OS' (CES 2026) + AI Engineering Copilot move the moat into AI-native software. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 8/10

  • Real physical-AI leverage — the automation + digital-twin + AI layer is exactly where humanoids monetize; Erlangen pilot (Humanoid HMND 01 on Jetson Thor) hit >90% autonomous pick success, targeting the 'world's first fully AI-driven adaptive manufacturing site' in 2026. ↗
  • Portfolio sharpening funds the pivot (Innomotics sold €3.5B, Healthineers deconsolidation). ↗

C · Track Record — 8/10

  • Built Xcelerator+Mendix into a genuine industrial-software franchise; the NVIDIA relationship has compounded (metaverse→digital twins→Industrial AI OS); moved from concept to live humanoid pilot with hard KPIs in months. ↗
  • But DI revenue fell ~10% in a FY25 downturn — cyclical execution isn't flawless.

Risks / bear case

  • Cyclicality — short-cycle automation (China/factory capex) drove a FY25 trough.
  • AI dependence on NVIDIA; not a robot maker (upside indirect vs pure-plays).
#2 Deere & Company DE · NYSE
Edge 9Capacity 8Track 8S · 83$169.2B · 4.8x · Fair
The clearest example in the universe of deployed, revenue-generating robotics at fleet scale — vision (See & Spray, 5M acres) and autonomy (9RX) backed by an unmatched data-plus-dealer moat ag peers can't quickly replicate. The honest discount is that full autonomy remains a measured, still-small rollout exposed to a cyclical downturn.

A · Leading-Edge — 9/10

  • Second-gen autonomy stack shipping, not slideware — Autonomous 9RX (up to 830hp, 16-camera 360° perception), retrofittable on existing machines, expanding autonomy to 'every job a tractor does'; See & Spray computer vision ran 5M acres across 1,000+ machines in 2025 (externally-validated ~$30/acre savings). ↗
  • A decade of stacked M&A (Blue River, Bear Flag) + ~1M+ connected machines / ~500M engaged acres = a proprietary training-data flywheel peers can't replicate. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 8/10

  • Full autonomous corn/soybean production system targeted by 2030; adjacency expansion (orchard sprayer, quarry dump truck, a commercial mower targeting a $50B landscaping-labor market); Solutions-as-a-Service targeting ~$5B (10% of sales) by 2030 — converting robotics into recurring revenue. ↗
  • Massive installed base as a retrofit distribution channel; structural farm-labor scarcity is the demand driver.

C · Track Record — 8/10

  • Delivered on prior commitments (2022 8R promise → 2025 tillage release → 2026 broader); See & Spray's 3x adoption proves pilot-to-fleet execution; kept autonomy funded through a downturn (FY25 revenue -12%). ↗
  • But only 'dozens' of autonomous tractors in real daily use — deployment is deliberate and still small.

Risks / bear case

  • Ag cycle is the master variable — a prolonged downturn slows the upgrade cycle autonomy rides on.
  • Sensor limits (dust/weather/GPS-denied) unsolved for hands-off scale; $5B services target unproven.

#1 Intuitive Surgical ISRG · NASDAQ
Edge 9Capacity 8Track 9S · 87$143.8B · 13.4x · Fair
The single most-validated embodied-AI robotics platform on the market — a profitable, cash-generative, decades-lead incumbent whose installed base, recurring-instrument model and unmatched surgical dataset compound into a genuine moat. Competition is finally arriving and the stock has de-rated, but nothing in the data suggests the flywheel is breaking; it's accelerating.

A · Leading-Edge — 9/10

  • Dominant installed base — 11,395 da Vinci systems (+12%) + 1,041 Ion; structural switching costs (years of surgeon-team training anchor OR workflow); 10M+ cumulative procedures feed an unmatched data flywheel (Case Insights). ↗
  • da Vinci 5 is a genuine leap (10,000x the compute of Xi, unique hardware Force Feedback cutting tissue force up to 43%); decades of FDA clearances/clinical evidence are a regulatory moat rivals must rebuild from scratch. ↗

B · Opportunity Capacity — 8/10

  • Razor-and-blade recurring model (instruments scale with procedure volume, +16% da Vinci / +39% Ion in Q1'26); large under-penetrated TAM (only ~300 procedures/system/yr); Ion (lung biopsy) is a second scaled platform; telesurgery/autonomy-assist optionality few can pursue at scale. ↗
  • Ceiling short of 10 only because surgical robotics is gated by regulation/capital budgets/adoption cycles — deliberate, not viral.

C · Track Record — 9/10

  • Rare profitable-at-scale robotics company — 2025 revenue ~$10.06B (+21%), ~67.6% GM, ~28% net margin; Q1'26 revenue +23%; da Vinci 5 ramp executing (870 units in 2025 vs 362); cash-generative with buybacks. ↗
  • Guiding double-digit procedure growth for 2026 — demand, not hype, driving the model.

Risks / bear case

  • Competition finally real (Medtronic Hugo cleared for urology Dec'25, J&J Ottava in trials, CMR, Chinese entrants) — 2026 is the first year of meaningful US competition.
  • Premium valuation (de-rated ~33% from highs) leaves little room for procedure-growth deceleration or dV5 margin drag.
